strengths: Addresses a genuine problem: making Equilibrium Propagation practical with achieved 10-100x speedup over P-EP
Comprehensive ablation studies across multiple architectures, depths, and connection types with thorough appendix analysis
Provides theoretical insights via Lyapunov exponent analysis (MLE/FTMLE) explaining convergence improvements
Clear presentation of methods with pseudocode (Algorithm 1) and implementation details enabling reproduction
Solid technical execution with appropriate statistical rigor (5 repetitions with standard deviations)
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Evaluation limited to MNIST and Fashion-MNIST only—insufficient for claiming 'practical' applicability in 2025. No evaluation on CIFAR-10, ImageNet, or realistic benchmarks makes the practical impact unclear

CRITICAL: Table 1 comparisons are unfair—different optimizers (SGD vs Adam), batch sizes (20 vs 500), and learning rates conflate effects. When 'Ours-DLR' uses identical P-EP hyperparameters, speedup is much less dramatic (1:01 vs 8:27). Paper fails to isolate contributions of feedback scaling vs optimizer vs batch size

No clear practical advantage over backpropagation: comparable/worse accuracy (97.5% vs 97.6% on MNIST within noise), still requires T+K iterative steps unlike BP's single pass, unclear when practitioners would use this instead of BP

Biological plausibility claims significantly overstated: feedback scaling is simply a hyperparameter tuning (not dynamic regulation), residual connections are standard technique (He et al. 2016), random skip connections with 20% probability do not plausibly represent cortical organization

Gradient vanishing trade-off incompletely addressed: weak feedback causes severe gradient vanishing (Figures S5-S6), residual connection fix doesn't fully recover performance (97.52% vs 97.61% BP), and represents ad-hoc compensation rather than principled solution

Hyperparameter sensitivity without principled selection: optimal β_i varies strongly with network depth and connection type; no systematic method provided for choosing β_i on new problems beyond extensive ablation

Table 2 concerning results unexplained: asymmetric 10-layer without residuals achieves 87.37% vs FA's 94.52% (huge gap); AGT variant fixes this via random skip connections (96.71%) but reproducibility unclear without seed specification

Limited novelty: feedback scaling is standard RNN technique (Bai et al. 2012; Liu et al. 2025), residual connections standard (He et al. 2016); contribution is primarily engineering showing combination works for EP

Theoretical contribution unclear: infinitesimal limit analysis (Appendix) is relegated to appendix, assumes weak feedback/supervision limits potentially violated in practice, provides post-hoc justification rather than principled derivation
Reproducibility concerns: code not actually available (only promised), training details scattered across Table S3, different computational environments reported, no systematic hyperparameter guidance

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine impracticality of Equilibrium Propagation
Comprehensive empirical analysis with extensive ablations and Lyapunov exponent characterization
Evaluation across multiple architectures (layered, convolutional, arbitrary topology)
Mathematical derivation of EP equivalence to BP/LRA under weak feedback limit
Clear presentation with detailed algorithms and informative supplementary materials
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core contributions reduce to spectral radius tuning and applying residual connections, both established techniques
Evaluation restricted to MNIST and Fashion-MNIST only; no realistic datasets (CIFAR-10, ImageNet) or neuromorphic hardware deployment
Unfair experimental comparisons: Table 1 uses different optimizers (Adam vs SGD), batch sizes (500 vs 20), and learning rates; speedup attribution unclear
Performance claims unsupported: Table 2 shows 10% error gaps for 10-layer networks without residuals (87.37% vs 97.61% BP); residuals become necessary crutch
Severe hyperparameter sensitivity with no principled selection method: optimal β_i varies across depths (0.01 for 2/10-layer, 0.1 for 5-layer)
Fundamental unresolved trade-off: weak feedback improves convergence but causes gradient vanishing; residuals patch rather than solve
Weak biological plausibility: feedback scaling is engineering trick not bio-inspired; random 20% skip connections lack justification
Missing critical ablations: no isolated evaluation of feedback scaling vs residuals; no analysis of why weak feedback helps beyond spectral radius reduction
Reproducibility issues: code not provided, different hardware for different experiments, many unjustified hyperparameter choices
Different activation functions vs baselines (tanh vs sigmoid-s) and learning rate schemes (uniform vs layer-specific in Ours-DLR) confound comparisons

strengths: Addresses an important problem: making Equilibrium Propagation practical is valuable for the biologically plausible learning community
Comprehensive experimental analysis including systematic ablations, Lyapunov exponent dynamics characterization, and evaluation across multiple architectures
Demonstrates significant practical speedups (~100x vs P-EP on MNIST) while maintaining competitive accuracy with backpropagation
Well-motivated from neuroscience with clear presentation connecting feedback regulation to biological observations (feedback-dominant regimes in cortex)
Theoretical contribution showing equivalence of EP, LRA, and BP under infinitesimal inference limits (Appendix)
Extends EP to deeper networks (10-layer) with residual connections, showing 5-7% accuracy improvements
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: only MNIST and Fashion-MNIST (28×28 images). No evaluation on CIFAR-10, ImageNet, or other realistic datasets. Claims about 'large-scale networks' are unsupported

Unfair comparison with P-EP: Table 1 conflates multiple confounding changes (batch size 20→500, optimizer SGD→Adam, learning rates, T/K schedules). The more conservative 'Ours-DLR' row matching P-EP parameters shows only 8.3x speedup vs claimed ~90x, undermining the main speedup claim

Biological plausibility claims are overstated: still uses softmax, Adam optimizer, full-precision arithmetic, and GPU computation. No demonstration on actual neuromorphic hardware or hardware-constrained benchmarks

Limited technical novelty: feedback scaling is well-established (Bai et al. 2012), residual connections are standard (He et al. 2016), and arbitrary topologies are from prior work (Salvatori et al. 2022). Contribution is primarily combining existing techniques
Hyperparameter sensitivity: βᵢ requires depth-dependent tuning (0.01 for 2-layer, 0.1 for 5-10 layers). No principled method provided for setting βᵢ on new problems, limiting practical applicability
Theory-practice gap: Appendix derives equivalence under infinitesimal limits (β→0) but experiments use β=0.01-0.1. Unclear how well theory justifies practical choices
Asymmetric weights severely underperform (10% gap for 10-layer networks: 87.37% vs 97.52%), which is problematic since symmetric weights are less biologically plausible (require weight transport)

Missing critical experimental comparisons: no head-to-head evaluation against other biologically plausible methods (LRA, recent EP variants, Scellier et al. 2023), limiting evidence for the approach's competitiveness
Code unavailable: stated 'available at' with no URL provided, severely impacting reproducibility
Mechanistic understanding incomplete: paper shows feedback scaling reduces Lyapunov exponents but doesn't rigorously explain why weak feedback approximates BP beyond infinitesimal assumptions

strengths: Comprehensive experimental analysis with systematic ablations on feedback/feedforward scaling, Lyapunov exponents, and network dynamics across multiple depths (2-20 layers) and architectures
Achieves substantial speedup (1-2 orders of magnitude) over prior EP work (P-EP), addressing genuine practical limitations of existing implementations
Rigorous theoretical grounding with formal analysis of EP equivalence to BP under weak feedback limits (Appendix C), supported by empirical validation
Strong reproducibility emphasis: detailed algorithms, hyperparameter specifications, promised code availability, and Jupyter notebooks for reproduction
Clear problem identification and well-motivated solutions grounded in neurobiology (feedback regulation in cortex, skip connections in cortical circuits)
Well-organized presentation with clear writing and informative figures demonstrating practical and theoretical insights
weaknesses: Limited novelty: applies well-known techniques (feedback scaling, residual connections) to existing algorithm; feedback weight scaling via spectral radius is standard RNN practice, residual connections are established since He et al. 2016

Critical hyperparameter sensitivity inadequately addressed: multiple hyperparameters (βᵢ, αᵢ, βf, P) optimized empirically with depth-dependent ranges (0.01-0.1 shallow, 0.1-0.25 deep); no principled selection method provided

Significant practical overhead vs. backpropagation persists despite speedup claims: 3HL is ~150x slower than BP (1:01:54 vs. 0:00:24), 2HL is ~4x slower, Conv is ~12x slower; 'orders of magnitude' speedup is relative to P-EP, not absolute

Limited scalability: notable accuracy gaps on CIFAR-10 in deep networks; applicability to deep CNNs explicitly unresolved; no evaluation on ImageNet or larger datasets; 20-layer network is shallow by modern standards

Incomplete vanishing gradient solution: weak feedback (small βᵢ) causes vanishing gradients, addressed by adding residual connections, creating an unresolved trade-off; asymmetric random graph topologies (20% connections) appear unmotivated beyond empirical results

Noise robustness degrades significantly with depth due to layer-wise accumulation; precision requirements (float64 for weak feedback) limit neuromorphic hardware implementation despite stated motivation
Feedback connections remain fixed during training without justification, deviating from standard EP in vector field dynamics; biological plausibility of this design choice not adequately explained

Biological plausibility claims overstated: constant scaling of fixed feedback weights is simplistic relative to complex cortical feedback regulation; random 20% asymmetric connectivity lacks biological grounding

strengths: Addresses real problem: accelerates EP training by orders of magnitude (50-100× speedup in wall-clock time)
Thorough experimental analysis with extensive ablations, Lyapunov exponent measurements, and noise robustness studies
Theoretical contribution in Appendix C showing equivalence between weak-feedback EP, LRA, and BP under infinitesimal inference limit
Comprehensive evaluation across layered and convolutional architectures with reproducible code and detailed hyperparameters
Clear motivation from neuroscience literature on feedback regulation and residual connections in cortical circuits
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: feedback scaling is straightforward hyperparameter tuning, residual connections well-established; combination is incremental

Biological plausibility claims fundamentally undermined: weak feedback (β_i=0.01-0.1) makes network behave like feedforward system, as confirmed by own theoretical analysis (Appendix C) and gradient similarity to BP (Figure S10)
Unresolved core tension: if weak-feedback EP≈BP theoretically, why keep two-phase learning? This undermines the entire biological plausibility motivation and raises whether standard BP is preferable
Unfair experimental comparisons with BP: different optimizers (Adam vs SGD), batch sizes (128-500 vs 20), learning rates (uniform vs per-layer), epochs, making speedup attribution ambiguous

Significantly worse performance on complex tasks: CIFAR-10 shows 14-44% accuracy gap vs BP (30.94% asymmetric vs 75.45% BP convolutional); impractical for real applications, attributed to 'inaccurate gradient approximation' without investigation

Unresolved hyperparameter sensitivity: β_i requires architecture-specific tuning (0.01 shallow, 0.1-0.25 deep) with no principled selection method; authors acknowledge 'finding a general way...is still on-going'
Incomplete residual connection design: no principled topology selection; empirical peak at P=20% (Figure S8) unexplained; residuals hurt shallow networks; asymmetric networks remain weak

Limited experimental scope: only MNIST and CIFAR-10 on tiny networks (~1-2K parameters); no modern architectures, large-scale tasks, or neuromorphic hardware validation despite claiming hardware motivation
Robustness concerns: severe degradation with time-varying state noise during training (Appendix C.6) raises questions about physical implementation
Missing critical baseline: no direct comparison between weak-feedback EP and standard BP applied to feedforward network with residuals—the ablation suggested by own theory

Incomplete literature comparison: concurrent methods (Liu et al. 2026, Laborieux & Zenke 2024) mentioned but not quantitatively compared; no systematic comparison with other biologically plausible algorithms

strengths: Addresses important practical problem of making Equilibrium Propagation feasible; achieves ~100x speedup over prior EP implementations
Comprehensive experimental analysis including ablation studies, Lyapunov exponent analysis, and multiple network depths; systematic exploration of feedback/feedforward scaling
Well-grounded in neuroscience literature with clear motivation from brain dynamics and cortical architecture
Significant wall-clock time improvements demonstrated (e.g., 1:56→0:01:16 for 2HL, 8:27→1:01:54 for 3HL)
Strong theoretical analysis connecting to BP and LRA under weak supervision regime; detailed mathematical derivations in appendices
Good reproducibility: detailed algorithms, hyperparameters, and code availability promised
weaknesses: Substantial performance gap on complex tasks: CIFAR-10 with 10-layer symmetric shows 13.3% absolute accuracy gap vs BP (48.23% vs 34.90%); authors acknowledge but don't adequately address this limitation

Hyperparameter β_i requires empirical tuning without principled selection method; different values needed for different architectures (0.01-0.1 for shallow vs 0.1-0.25 for convolutional) undermining 'practical' claims
Unfair experimental comparisons: P-EP vs FRE-RNN use different optimizers (SGD vs Adam), batch sizes (20 vs 500), epochs, and learning schedules; difficult to isolate contribution of proposed method

Limited experimental scope: only MNIST and CIFAR-10 on small networks (64 neurons/layer, ≤20 layers); no ImageNet or realistic modern datasets; authors explicitly state deep CNN applicability 'remains to be explored'
Weak performance with asymmetric connections (more biologically plausible): 10-layer asymmetric CIFAR-10 achieves 30.37% (Ours) vs 37.97% (FA), contradicting bio-plausibility claims
Limited novelty: feedback scaling via spectral radius and residual connections are well-established; main contribution is application to EP which is somewhat incremental
Gradient flow remains problematic despite residual connections: Figures S5-S6 show persistent layer-wise error differences (orders of magnitude), suggesting learning remains hierarchical not local

Overstated claims: abstract claims 'performance on par with backpropagation' and 'substantially enhances applicability' misleading given deep network limitations; equivalence to BP relies on infinitesimal limits not holding in practice
Unfair comparisons with P-EP: different optimizers, batch sizes, and epochs make speedup attribution unclear; 'Ours-DLR' variant attempts fairness but limited in scope
State noise robustness degrades significantly in deeper networks (Section C.6), limiting viability for neuromorphic hardware implementations
